title: Congee
subtitle: plain rice porridge with ginger, spring onion and sesame oil
excerpt: Silky rice porridge simmered low and slow until each grain has dissolved into a creamy, comforting bowl. Topped simply with fresh ginger, spring onion and white pepper. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Congee, or zhou in Mandarin, is one of the oldest rice preparations in China, with references in texts dating to the Zhou dynasty. It is eaten across East and South-East Asia under different names: jook in Cantonese, kayu in Japanese, cháo in Vietnamese. The plain version with simple toppings is the Cantonese standard and is documented in countless Chinese cookbooks of the twentieth century. It is served for breakfast, as a restorative meal when ill, and as a late-night comfort food.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Congee thickens as it sits. Reheat with extra water or stock, stirring, until it returns to a pourable consistency.

glossaryTerms.definition: A rice porridge made by simmering rice in a large quantity of water or stock until the grains break down and the liquid becomes thick and creamy. Eaten across East and South-East Asia. The ratio of rice to water is typically 1:10 for a creamy result.

A long-grain fragrant rice variety common in Thai and southern Chinese cooking. It has a slightly floral aroma when cooked. For congee, it breaks down faster than standard long-grain rice, producing a silkier texture.

Ground from the inner seed of the pepper berry with the outer hull removed. It has a sharper, more pungent heat than black pepper and is used in Chinese and South-East Asian cooking. A standard seasoning for congee and egg dishes.

A dark, fragrant oil pressed from toasted sesame seeds. Used as a finishing condiment rather than a cooking oil, as its flavour diminishes under direct heat. A small amount adds a characteristic nutty aroma.

items.prepNote: half minced for cooking, half cut into fine matchsticks for topping

content.text: Rinse the rice in several changes of cold water until the water runs mostly clear. Drain.
Combine the rice, chicken stock, minced ginger and 1 litre of water in a large pot. Bring to the boil over high heat.
Reduce to a low simmer. Cook uncovered, stirring every 10 minutes, for 60 to 70 minutes until the rice has completely broken down and the congee is thick and creamy.
Ladle into bowls. Top with ginger matchsticks, spring onions, a drizzle of sesame oil and white pepper. Add a splash of soy sauce if you like.

items.symptom: Rice is catching on the bottom of the pot
items.cause: Heat is too high or the pot is thin-bottomed.
items.fix: Keep the heat at a very gentle simmer and stir every 10 minutes. A heavy-bottomed pot makes a real difference.

items.symptom: Congee is too thin after 70 minutes
items.cause: The simmer was too low or the pot was covered.
items.fix: Cook uncovered at a slightly higher heat for another 10 to 15 minutes, stirring regularly.

items.cause: It has thickened too much or sat off the heat.
items.fix: Stir in hot water or stock a ladleful at a time until it loosens to a pourable consistency.

content.text: Congee is one of the most widely eaten dishes across China and much of Asia, and has been for thousands of years. The plain version is a blank canvas: eaten for breakfast with pickles and youtiao (fried dough sticks), served as recovery food when someone is ill, or made richer with century egg, minced pork or fresh fish. Its simplicity is part of the point. A good congee requires patience rather than skill.
